questions.q: What is the main difference between Classic Encryption and Shield Platform Encryption?
options: They are identical features with different names
Classic Encryption only works on Opportunity records; Shield Platform Encryption only works on custom objects
Classic Encryption is an older, more limited capability (narrow field types, weaker encryption, no files/attachments); Shield Platform Encryption is the modern AES-256 option with broader coverage
Shield Platform Encryption does not support customer-managed key material, while Classic Encryption does
questions.explain: Classic Encryption is the older, more limited capability -- narrower field type coverage, weaker encryption, no file/attachment support. Shield Platform Encryption is the modern, far more capable AES-256 option that current architecture designs are built around.

questions.q: A field needs to support exact-match filtering in list views and reports. Which encryption scheme supports that, and why?
options: Probabilistic, because randomness makes filtering easier
Classic Encryption, because it was designed specifically for filterable fields
Neither scheme supports any filtering once a field is encrypted
Deterministic, because it always produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext, which is what allows exact-match comparison
questions.explain: Deterministic encryption always produces identical ciphertext for identical plaintext, which is exactly what makes exact-match filtering, list views, and some report filters possible -- probabilistic encryption's randomness makes that kind of comparison impossible.

questions.q: What real security/functionality tradeoff does choosing deterministic encryption over probabilistic encryption involve?
options: Deterministic encryption enables exact-match filtering, but because equal values always produce identical ciphertext, it is more exposed to certain pattern-based inference than probabilistic encryption
Deterministic encryption is always slower to query than probabilistic encryption
There is no tradeoff -- deterministic encryption is strictly better in every respect
Deterministic encryption cannot be applied to custom fields, only standard fields
questions.explain: The tradeoff is explicit: deterministic's identical ciphertext for identical plaintext is what enables filtering, but that same consistency makes it more exposed to pattern-based inference than the randomized probabilistic scheme.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a "tenant secret" in Shield Platform Encryption's key-management model?
options: A password shared between all Salesforce customers
The customer-controlled layer of key material, generated and managed by the org's own administrators through Setup, that determines what the org's data is actually encrypted with
A hidden Salesforce feature with no customer visibility or control
The name of the encryption algorithm itself
questions.explain: The tenant secret is the layer an org's own administrators control through Setup -- generating, rotating, and managing the key material that determines what their data is encrypted with, separate from Salesforce's own internally managed root-level secret.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend testing an encryption rollout thoroughly in a sandbox before enabling it in production?
options: Because encryption cannot be reversed once enabled under any circumstances
Because sandboxes have faster encryption algorithms than production orgs

Because encrypting a field can affect search, formula fields, sorting, managed package compatibility, and because disabling encryption later may not remove every restriction that was introduced while it was enabled
Because Salesforce requires a sandbox test as a formal compliance step for every org
questions.explain: Several real side effects (search behavior, formula fields, managed package compatibility, and restrictions that can outlast the encryption setting itself) make sandbox testing the practical way to catch surprises before they affect a live production org.
